title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). Two preregistered design choices—shared_initial_generation (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions) and reuse of the same deterministic validator as both the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer—produced a deterministic ceiling effect in this run that rendered the primary estimand uninformative for assessing generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics. The preregistered design (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt‑5‑mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime guard and scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes) and shared_initial_generation semantics. Confirmatory outcomes (archived artifacts) show complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). We present the preregistered methodology, the exact artifact‑grounded results, a diagnostic analysis explaining why the design choices produced a ceiling, and concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into network configuration artifacts and staged change workflows (canaries, progressive rollout, rollback). Prior work shows LLMs can produce syntactically plausible configuration templates in controlled settings while verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops and deterministic network verifiers reduce syntactic and semantic errors in IaC and related domains. The operational safety question for agentic NetOps pipelines is end‑to‑end: how do generator variability, runtime verification, staged rollout semantics, repair, and rollback interact to affect safe‑deploy outcomes? We ask: under the benchmark semantics used here, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) measured on N=400 preregistered paired tasks.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; (2) exact, archive‑verifiable confirmatory results showing universal acceptance of shared generator outputs by the deterministic validator (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0); (3) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis demonstrating that preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics combined with reusing a single deterministic validator produced a deterministic ceiling that makes the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard interaction in this run; and (4) concrete, implementable benchmark‑hardening recommendations grounded in the archived traces.
sections.related_work: We situate this experiment at the intersection of intent→configuration generation, verifier‑guided IaC workflows, deterministic network verification, and agentic/tool‑augmented LLM systems. Representative verified prior works include: intent‑to‑configuration evaluations showing LLMs can synthesize usable configuration templates [Nguyen et al., 2024], studies of LLMs applied to Infrastructure as Code and automated configuration synthesis [Li et al., 2024], verifier‑guided IaC systems that use verifier feedback to improve correctness (TerraFormer) [Jana et al., 2026], deterministic network verification and reachability tools for network checks [Liu et al., 2025], and surveys/architectural discussions of agentic/tool‑augmented LLM workflows in AIOps and NetOps that document both benefits and new failure modes [Pei et al., 2025; Taparia et al., 2026]. These works motivate closed‑loop generator+guard evaluations but also highlight gaps: community‑standard, action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollouts, repair, rollback, and provenance are limited. Our study operationalizes a compact action‑aware staging benchmark under a strict preregistered design to probe verifier utility under those constraints and to surface practical design pitfalls.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The study was preregistered (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1). The primary confirmatory estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (two‑sided inference, α=0.05). The preregistered analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) implements a permutation‑based paired difference test and reports exact permutation p‑values; the exact McNemar two‑sided test was produced for corroboration. Bootstrap percentile 95% confidence intervals (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) were frozen for secondary outcomes.

Adapter semantics and shared generation (design note). Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer. Critically, the preregistration set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): each task provoked a single deterministic LLM generation that was delivered identically to both the baseline and guarded episodes. We explicitly state here (as required): under these two preregistered design choices—shared_initial_generation and reuse of deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both runtime guard and scorer—the primary estimand was rendered effectively untestable in this execution because the guard had no opportunity to act on distinct generator outputs.

Episode flow, validator policy, and repair rules. For each task the adapter requested a single shared candidate from gpt‑5‑mini, delivered that candidate to both episodes, and (in the guarded episode) routed the candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which applied full intent‑constraint validation using a deterministic rule set recorded in validator_trace entries. The preregistered repair policy permitted up to one repair attempt in the guarded episode; repair invocations, repair_applied flags, validation_before/after states, and final validity decisions were recorded. In this execution repair_applied = false across all episodes.

Task generation, difficulty metadata, and deterministic replay. Tasks were generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each task record contains structured difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, pattern, required_command_count, and level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). The preregistration required deterministic three‑replay consistency checks for each agent+simulator pair; any pair failing replay or encountering simulator errors would be flagged and excluded per the missingness_plan. All three‑replay checks passed and no exclusions were applied (complete_pairs = 400).

Analysis plan. The primary analysis used exact permutation on paired safe‑deploy booleans (α=0.05). The exact McNemar test was reported for corroboration. Secondary outcomes included bootstrap CI for median time‑to‑rollback and counts of repair attempts; preregistered sensitivity analyses (treating excluded pairs as failures or restricted permutations) were available but unnecessary because there were no exclusions. All analysis code, seeds, and logs are archived in the analysis artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and reconciliation. The run started 2026‑08‑29T18:23:37Z and completed 2026‑08‑29T19:12:38Z. Planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 400 (shared initial generation); complete_pairs = 400. Deterministic three‑replay checks passed for all pairs; no exclusions were recorded. (See Table 1 for the execution summary.)

Primary confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑grounded). The primary contingency counts were baseline_success_count = 400 (baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and guarded_success_count = 400 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n_11 = 400 with n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0, yielding observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. The preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0; the exact McNemar two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Cohen's h = 0.0. These numbers are reproduced directly from the archived analysis artifacts (analysis/*).

Repair, rollback, and validator traces. Across the 800 episodes repair_applied = false and no rollbacks were invoked; validator_trace entries show validation_after.final_state matched expected_final_state for accepted configurations. This explains universal acceptance: when the shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5, both episodes necessarily recorded safe‑deploy outcomes.

Task difficulty metadata and representative patterns. Every task record in execution/task_manifest.jsonl contains a difficulty label. Representative sample entries among the first six archived tasks show one medium, two hard, and three very_hard patterns; these representative examples are included in the archived artifact bundle. The full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 tasks are archived and available for aggregation by auditors (execution/task_manifest.jsonl). The artifact bundle contains the raw task manifest; the manuscript does not invent additional aggregated counts beyond the archived representative sample because a verified aggregated per‑level tally was not precomputed in the archived analysis artifacts.

Worked example (representative pair). Pair pair‑000001 (task‑000001) illustrates the shared‑candidate flow: the shared LLM candidate was

interface edge1 admin down
interface edge1 vlan 30
interface edge1 mtu 1600
interface edge1 admin up

The validator_trace for this pair records parsed_command_count=4, required_command_count=4, valid=true, repair_applied=false, and final_state matching the expected_final_state; both baseline and guarded episodes accepted the shared candidate and scored as safe_deploy=1 in the archived scoring artifacts (see execution/scoring/task‑000001‑*.json in the artifact bundle).

Statistical interpretation. The observed ceiling collapses inferential variance: permutation and McNemar tests correctly report p = 1.0, but those statistics do not provide evidence about generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics because the design prevented the guard from having an opportunity to intervene. The preregistered power calculation assumed within‑pair variability that did not occur; those assumptions are invalidated by the deterministic ceiling and therefore the original power rationale does not apply to these results.
sections.discussion:
Design diagnosis. Two preregistered design choices produced the deterministic ceiling. First, shared_initial_generation intentionally removed generator variance by delivering identical LLM outputs to baseline and guarded episodes. Second, the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When the deterministic validator accepts the shared candidate, both conditions record identical safe‑deploy outcomes and the paired difference must be zero. This is a construct‑validity outcome of the frozen design, not a general null statement about verifier utility across diverse generator/validator pairings.

Consequences and recommendations. Because the preregistered design eliminated generation variance, the study cannot adjudicate whether a runtime guard would improve outcomes under alternative designs. Using archived validator_trace and execution accounting we recommend concrete, implementable changes for future preregistered runs that preserve signal for generator×guard interactions:

1) Independent per‑condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true) so each condition receives independently sampled generator outputs and the guard has bona fide opportunities to accept, block, or request repair.

2) Distinct runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer implementations (or a held‑out scorer) to prevent conflation of runtime acceptance and analysis scoring; archived validator_trace entries show acceptance decisions and validation states—using a separate scorer preserves adjudication.

3) Controlled adversarial seeding: preregister a controlled fraction of perturbation seeds that produce nontrivial baseline failure rates to preserve power. The task manifest supports seeding and deterministic generation, enabling reproducible adversarial injection.

4) Difficulty‑stratified sampling: ensure the benchmark composition contains a sufficient proportion of very_hard tasks to produce measurable baseline errors; per‑task difficulty metadata are archived and can be sampled deterministically.

5) Instrument and record repair attempts, repairs applied, and time‑to‑rollback as preregistered secondary outcomes (these fields are already present in validator_trace entries and repair logs in the artifact bundle).

Operational implications. For NetOps practitioners: (i) experiment designs that remove generation variance can hide the potential benefits of runtime guards; and (ii) independent adjudication channels (distinct scorers or human reviewers) are important for measuring guard impact.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on an action‑aware staging benchmark. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling effect resulted from frozen design and implementation homogeneity and renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to support hardened follow‑on experiments (independent generation, adversarial seeding, heterogeneous validators) that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors. The artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations supplied here offer concrete steps researchers can preregister to preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility in NetOps settings.

Reproducibility note. All execution and analysis artifacts supporting the numbers and traces reported here are archived in the bundled artifact set (execution/* and analysis/*). Key artifacts produced by the run include the execution manifest, raw results, model configuration, deterministic validator traces, the task manifest with per‑task difficulty metadata, and the analysis results (paired contingency and bootstrap outputs). These artifacts contain the seeds, deterministic replay checks, and the validator_trace records that underpin the diagnosis and recommendations above; auditors can reproduce the reported summaries using the archived manifests and analysis code as recorded in the artifact bundle.

Final interpretive boundary. The null paired difference observed here is a valid, artifact‑grounded outcome for the preregistered design. It should not be interpreted as evidence that runtime verification is unnecessary in general. Instead, it illustrates how specific preregistered design choices (shared generation and reuse of the same deterministic validator for runtime and scoring) can eliminate the statistical signal needed to evaluate generator×guard closed‑loop effects. Evaluations that wish to measure guard utility must preserve generator variance and independent adjudication as described above.

Orchestration: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with shared_initial_generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) as preregistered. Runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Preregistration: cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1 (preregistration SHA‑256 recorded in the execution manifest). The immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. Topic constraints were selected pre‑lock by the Research Director and limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focused on reliability/safety of intent→configuration generation. The guarded condition routed the shared LLM candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which deterministically accepted or blocked candidates per the preregistered adapter policy; the adapter allowed up to one repair call per task but no repairs were applied (repair_applied = false across episodes). limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and can be aggregated by auditors; this manuscript reports representative sample counts (e.g., among the first six archived tasks: one medium, two hard, three very_hard) but does not invent aggregated counts absent an explicit verified aggregate in the archived analysis artifacts.
